text.p: The decision by European drugs groups Bayer AG and Roche Holding AG's to join forces in the U.S. over-the-counter drugs market does not mean further cooperation in Europe, analysts said on Tuesday.

The German and Swiss industry powerhouses on Monday unveiled plans to form a 50-50 joint venture selling pain killers and gynaecological drugs in United States, lifting Bayer to one of the top five OTC firms from 15th.

Analysts welcomed the step, which brought together several struggling products to try gain better footing in the lucrative and highly competitive American OTC market but said it would likely remain a one-off deal.

"The key with this deal is that each company is retaining its star products to sell them separately in the U.S., indicating the deal does not have a major strategic component," said Thomas Schiessle, analyst at Delbrueck & Co. in Frankfurt.
Bayer will continue to sell its high profile Bayer aspirin, Alka-Seltzer, One-A-Day and Flintstones vitamins on its own while Roche will keep its vitamins.
OTC drugs are sold without a physician's prescription.

If the two companies had envisioned laying the groundwork for a broader global cooperation with their U.S. step, analysts agreed they would likely have thrown the star performers into the deal from the beginning.

As the deal appears constructed mainly to improve sales and marketing operations for brands like Roche's Aleve analgesic and Bayer's Midol menstrual pain drug and analysts see little impact on either group's share price or results.
In dissecting the motivation for the deal, analysts agree that Roche may stand to benefit more since it was eager to obtain a sales and marketing organisation in the U.S.
"It was a logical step to take given the size of (Roche's) OTC business in the U.S.," said Steve Putnam, analyst at Kleinwort Benson in London.

The two European companies may have agreed to terms more quickly because they were both small outsiders in the U.S. market and efforts to cooperate with a key U.S. player like Warner Lambert Co. would have been very costly, analyst said.
Now Bayer and Roche may have bought some breathing room, pushing pack the "day when they need to do something more aggressive," Putnam added.

But in Europe, the two face different circumstances with Bayer already well established and Roche showing little interest in expanding its small OTC business. Consequently analysts see little interest in a similar move in Europe.
"If Roche all the sudden tried to get a stronger foothold in the OTC market, that would be a strategic shift of policy," Schiessle said.
Bayer was not immediately available for comment on its goals for the OTC business in Europe and whether it was planning any joint ventures, possibly with other companies.
But Bankgesellschaft Berlin analyst Christa Baehr stressed, "the U.S. deal is a positive sign that further cooperation, possibly in other areas, could be expanded" between the two groups.
Especially in light of the general trend of consolidation in the chemical and drugs industry, Baehr added, more "steps could come much more quickly now."
